options: What is a compiler, an OS, a network?
What is computation? Which problems can a computer solve? Which can be solved efficiently?
How to code, test and deploy?
What are sets, functions and graphs?

01-course-introduction.q: What does the SE 3310 midterm cover?
options: Everything up to and including context-free grammars — not pushdown automata
Receive no marks — diagrams must be made with software (TikZ or Graphviz)

options: Hilbert's mechanical procedure for deciding any statement does not exist

options: False — ∅ has no elements, {∅} has exactly one (the empty set)

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.explain: Each element makes an independent in/out choice: 2⁴ = 16.

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.q: A = {x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄}. Which statement is TRUE?
02-notation-languages-and-dfas.explain: x₁ is an element, not a set. A proper subset must differ from A, but ⊆ allows equality.

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.q: How does a tuple differ from a set?
options: Tuples are ordered and allow repeats

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.q: For f : ℤ → ℤ with f(x) = x², what is the image?
02-notation-languages-and-dfas.explain: The codomain is declared (ℤ); the image is what's actually achieved.

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.q: Over Σ = {A…Z}, why is PASSWORD1 not a string?
With a = 00 and b = 11, what is (ab)²?
Σ* is infinite. Does it contain an infinitely long string?
options: No — every element of Σ* is finite; there's just no longest one

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.q: Formally, what is computation in this course?
options: Deciding, for a language L and string s, whether s ∈ L

02-notation-languages-and-dfas.q: What is the DFA transition function's signature?
The two-state DFA where 1 swaps states and 0 loops, accepting q₁: which string is accepted?
02-notation-languages-and-dfas.explain: It accepts an odd number of 1s. 111 has three.

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: A finite state transducer differs from a DFA because…
options: It produces output — edges are labelled input/output

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: What is step 1 of the DFA design checklist?
options: Ask what the machine must remember — each situation becomes a state

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: The "divisible by 4" DFA passes through the accepting state while reading 0100 but leaves it. What decides acceptance?
options: Any visit to an accept state
Only the state after the last symbol
A state that can never lead to an accepting state
An accepting state with no exits

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: True or false: every DFA diagram must draw a dead state.
options: False — δ just has to be total; missing arrows are conventionally read as going to an undrawn dead state
False — DFAs can't have dead states

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: Accepting EE or OO in the parity machine collapses to which language?
In the contains-11010 DFA, a mismatch in s5 (having read 1101, then 1) goes to s3, not s1. Why?
options: The text now ends in 11, which is still a prefix of 11010 — going to s1 would discard a real partial match

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: Reversing the 11010 DFA (swap start/accept, reverse arrows) produces…
options: A DFA for the same language
A machine for 01011 that is not a DFA — some states have two arrows for a symbol, others none

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: How many states does a DFA for "at least two 1s" need?
03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.explain: zero, one, two+ — beyond two, the exact count stops mattering.

03-regular-languages-and-dfa-constructio.q: For the ends-in-01 DFA, from the accepting state a 0 goes to…
options: The "...0" state — the 0 may begin the next 01
When at least one thread ends in an accepting state

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: What is the NFA transition function's signature?
δ(q, a) = ∅ in an NFA means…
options: That thread terminates; the computation continues if other threads are alive

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: True or false: an NFA rejects as soon as one thread dies.
options: False — rejection requires every thread to fail at the end

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: True or false: every DFA is an NFA.
options: True — a DFA is an NFA whose δ-sets have exactly one element and that never uses ε

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: Run the ends-in-01 NFA (q₀ loops; q₀ →0 q₁ →1 q₂) on 0110 by sets. Result?
options: Rejected — final set {q₀, q₁} has no q₂

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: An NFA for "contains s" for a pattern of length n always has how many states?
In the contains-11010 NFA, removing the loop on the start state q₀ changes the language to…
What is E({p}) if p →ε q →ε r?
04-non-determinism-and-nfas.explain: Chains count — keep following ε-arrows until nothing new appears.

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: E({q}) when no ε-arrow leaves q is…
What is the standard use of ε-transitions from a new start state?
options: Running two machines as one (union) without merging their states

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: The "lucky guess" interpretation of non-determinism involves…
options: No randomness — if an accepting path exists, the guess is defined to find it
Trying paths one at a time with backtracking

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: An NFA for "third-to-last symbol is 1" has 4 states. How many does the DFA need?
04-non-determinism-and-nfas.explain: It must remember the last three symbols: 2³ = 8.

04-non-determinism-and-nfas.q: A machine has an ε-arrow, some empty rows, and one row with two entries. It is…
options: A valid NFA but not a DFA

05-the-subset-construction.q: What does the subset construction prove?
options: Every DFA has an equivalent NFA
Every NFA has an equivalent DFA
NFAs are more powerful than DFAs

05-the-subset-construction.q: An NFA has 3 states. At most how many states can its subset DFA have?
What is the start state of the subset DFA?
05-the-subset-construction.explain: Forgetting the closure on the start state is the most common conversion mistake.

05-the-subset-construction.q: When is a subset state accepting?
options: When it contains at least one NFA accepting state
Only if it's the start state

05-the-subset-construction.q: How is a combined row like δ_D({q₀, q₁}, a) computed?
options: The union of the members' single-state rows

05-the-subset-construction.q: In Example 1, state 3 →a 1 and 1 →ε 3. What is δ_D({3}, a)?
05-the-subset-construction.explain: The closure applies after every step: E({1}) = {1, 3}.

05-the-subset-construction.q: In the subset DFA, the empty set ∅ is…
Does the subset construction ever change the language?
options: Never — the DFA state always equals the NFA's set of live states

05-the-subset-construction.q: Converting the ends-in-01 NFA yields how many reachable subset states?
05-the-subset-construction.explain: {q₀}, {q₀, q₁}, {q₀, q₂} — exactly Lecture 3's hand-built DFA, renamed.

05-the-subset-construction.q: Step 5 of the algorithm, mislabelled "minimization" on the slides, actually does what?
What does the equivalence of NFAs and DFAs buy you?
options: One notion of "regular", and the freedom to design with an NFA

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: To disprove a closure property, what suffices?
How do you complement a regular language?
options: Swap accept states of any NFA
Determinize to a DFA, then swap accepting and non-accepting states

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: Why doesn't swapping accept states work on an NFA?
options: A string may have accepting paths under both the original and swapped sets
A new start state with ε-arrows to both machines' start states
A product of the state sets

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: In the concatenation construction for L₂L₁, why are L₂'s accepting states demoted?
options: Otherwise bare L₂ strings with no L₁ part would be accepted
NFAs can only have one accept state

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: Why does the star construction add a NEW accepting start state rather than marking the old start accepting?
options: Computations can return to the old start mid-run and would then wrongly accept

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: How is closure under intersection proved?
options: De Morgan: L₁ ∩ L₂ = complement(L̄₁ ∪ L̄₂), using closure under complement and union
No — the first 0 is followed by a 0

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: What is ϕ* (star of the empty set)?
06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.explain: k = 0 blocks is always allowed and yields ε. But Rϕ = ϕ.

options: A language is regular iff some regular expression describes it

06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.q: The precedence in ab* ∪ c is…
06-closure-properties-and-regular-expres.explain: Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union.

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: Why is {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} not regular, intuitively?
options: Matching the counts requires remembering an unbounded number — finitely many states can't
Yes — it's finite (101 strings), and every finite language is regular

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: In the pumping lemma game, who chooses p and the split xyz?
07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.explain: Adversary: p and the split. You: s and i.

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: Why does the pumping lemma hold for regular languages?
options: Pigeonhole: reading p symbols on a p-state DFA visits some state twice, creating a loop

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: What does condition |xy| ≤ p buy you when s begins with 0ᵖ?
options: y must consist only of 0s — the case analysis collapses to one case

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: "Let p = 5 and s = 0⁵1⁵…" What's wrong with this proof?
options: p is the adversary's unknown number; fixing it proves nothing for larger machines

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: "Split s as x = ε, y = 0ᵖ, z = 1ᵖ; pumping gives 0²ᵖ1ᵖ ∉ L." What's wrong?
options: Only one split was defeated — you must defeat every legal split

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: You pumped every split of a string successfully. What have you proved?
For L = {0ᵐ1ⁿ : m > n}, which pump works with s = 0ᵖ⁺¹1ᵖ?
07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.explain: Pumping up only increases the surplus of 0s; deleting y removes it.

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: Prove "equally many 0s and 1s" (L₄) is non-regular without pumping. How?
options: If L₄ were regular, L₄ ∩ 0*1* = {0ⁿ1ⁿ} would be regular — contradiction

07-non-regular-languages-and-the-pumping.q: Which condition ensures pumping actually changes the string?
Which string is a legitimate choice for proving {0ⁿ1ⁿ} non-regular?

08-context-free-grammars.q: Why can a grammar describe {0ⁿ1ⁿ} when no DFA can?
options: It builds the string from the middle outward, pairing each 0 with its 1 at birth — no counting needed

08-context-free-grammars.q: In a derivation, the arrow ⇒ is used for ____ and → for ____.

When no variables remain — only terminals

Sentences must end with a period
